name: Elena Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a loading vehicle at a large mine, mostly shifting rock from the face to the haul trucks. I'm 43 and still junior enough that I ask the older operators to check my judgement on a bad slope. The cab smells of dust and warm plastic by lunch, but I like seeing a clean load leave without anyone rushing. At home my partner Marco and I have two children in school and a mortgage; the late shift makes homework night rather short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say a little software help is fine if the loader still needs a careful pair of hands. I already use AI on my phone to explain a warning light in plain words, then check the manual before touching anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I don't think the small saving in office time reaches my pay packet. Our mortgage payment doesn't become smaller because a clerk finishes a form faster. I have a few months of expenses set aside, and I don't like dipping into them for ordinary school bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking my shifts and checking the tyres before the morning load. This month I'll put the school costs on one page with Marco so we can see what is actually left after the mortgage. Then we'll set aside a small fixed amount from normal pay rather than rely on overtime. In the first year of this picture I'd still be operating the loader, not buying any fancy machine myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly I feel steady in the cab, and a bit pinched when the school sends another payment notice. The technology part doesn't frighten me in this picture; the household arithmetic does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you mean by school costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children have a bus pass and a sports fee due within weeks of each other. Last year we paid both out of savings, which is exactly the habit I want to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for more shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if there were a real gap after we wrote the numbers down. I won't promise the children a weekend away on the strength of overtime that hasn't been offered.

say: I would tell the crew **small software gains** are useful if the loader still needs care.
I use a phone tool for **warning lights**, then check the machine manual.
think: I doubt office savings will **raise my pay** at the mine.
Our **mortgage and school bills** make me guard the few months of savings we have.
do: Keep taking **loader shifts** and inspect tyres before morning loads.
Set aside a **small fixed amount** from normal pay after listing school costs with Marco.
feel: Steady about my work, but **pinched** by routine family costs.
S0.quote: Our mortgage payment doesn't become smaller because a clerk finishes a form faster.
fieldNote: Elena separates the minor **AI effect** from bills that already strain her household.
She uses a phone tool, but confirms every **machine warning** against the manual before acting.

steps.text: Keep taking loader shifts and inspect tyres before morning loads
Set aside a small fixed amount from normal pay after listing school costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that office buying and shift rosters may change before anyone replaces a loader. If the mine can cut paperwork, fair enough, but I want the new shift sheet posted where we can all see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, junior people get the awkward shifts when the office starts squeezing hours. I'm still learning the ground, so a supervisor could decide a smaller crew is enough if the planning gets faster. I can find another mine nearby, but another commute would take time from the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the shift supervisor this week how rosters will be set, and I'd practise using the mine's digital maintenance log with a senior operator. If my shifts fall in the first year, I'd apply to the other mine across the valley before using the school money. I'd keep our extra spending tight until I knew the hours were real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested in the new log and uneasy about who controls the roster. Learning a screen is easier than making a missing shift appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tight spending mean at your house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing would be the weekend trip we talked about for spring. I'd keep the bus passes and sports fee because those are the children's normal week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask that senior operator?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia, who has driven that section for years, knows which fault codes can wait and which mean stop. I'd ask her to sit beside me for one maintenance entry so I don't copy nonsense into the record.

say: I would say **office planning** may change before anyone replaces a loader.
I want every new **shift roster** posted where crews can check it.
think: My junior standing could mean **fewer shifts** if management runs a smaller crew.
Another local mine is possible, but its **commute** would take family time.
do: Ask the **shift supervisor** this week how rosters will be set.
Practise the **digital maintenance log** beside an experienced operator.
Apply to the **valley mine** if shifts fall, and cancel the spring trip.
feel: Curious about the log, but **uneasy** about control over hours.
S1.quote: Learning a screen is easier than making a missing shift appear.
fieldNote: Her willingness to learn does not erase the risk of **lost hours** for a junior operator.
She protects her children’s **weekly costs** while treating a spring trip as expendable.

steps.text: Practise the digital maintenance log with a senior operator
Apply to the mine across the valley if shifts fall
Cancel the planned spring weekend trip if hours shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the gate I'd say the clever planning system arrives in 2028, but a robot that can run our loaders as well as us is three years behind it. I'd ask the boss to tell us exactly which jobs disappear at each date, instead of putting up a cheerful poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, 2031 is close when you're 43 with a mortgage and two children in school. AI could take the planning and records in 2028, while I might still drive for three years; the hands-on work isn't safe after capable robots arrive. My few months of savings would not cover a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now by asking the training office about an equipment repair apprenticeship and whether the mine pays trainees. I'd keep driving and use the digital fault logs to learn what breaks, rather than pretend I can change trades overnight. In 2029, the first year after the thinking system, I'd ask for supervised repair hours and apply to local maintenance workshops if no paid place opens. After 2031 I'd seek paid repair work, even if it is outside the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened by the short clock, though I can still make calls and learn. I worry more about the mortgage date than about the machine itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would repair work also be exposed to the later robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably some of it, yes. I wouldn't call it a lifetime shelter, but a workshop may still pay someone to inspect and fix machines while I work out the next move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Marco, my partner, that the children can stay in their school for now but we must stop treating overtime as guaranteed. He'd want to see the apprenticeship pay before we changed any bill.

say: I would tell the crew **thinking AI** reaches planning in 2028 and capable loaders arrive around 2031.
I would press management for **specific job dates** rather than a reassuring poster.
think: I could keep driving for three years, but **robots threaten** my hands-on job after 2031.
A few months of savings cannot cover a **long search** with a mortgage.
do: Ask the training office about a **paid repair apprenticeship** now.
Keep driving while learning from **digital fault logs**.
Seek supervised repair hours in 2029 and apply to **local workshops** if needed.
feel: **Frightened** by the short clock, but still able to act.
S2.quote: My few months of savings would not cover a long search.
fieldNote: Elena names the **three-year gap** between desk systems and capable mining robots without treating it as permanent safety.
Her proposed apprenticeship depends on **trainee pay** because the mortgage makes unpaid study unrealistic.

steps.text: Ask the mine training office whether repair apprentices are paid
Keep driving the loader while learning from fault logs
Apply to local maintenance workshops if the mine offers no paid place

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to ask hard questions, not enough to trust a vague promise of jobs. The office work goes in 2031 and capable robots reach the pit around 2034, when my children will be teenagers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may have time to learn repair properly before the loaders change, but I cannot assume the mine will employ me for all five years. At 48 the mortgage will still be there, and my junior grade won't magically become senior because a course exists. Marco and I would need proof of wages before moving any money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the mine's paid trainee places with the two repair shops near the ring road this winter. If a paid place opens, I'd enrol and take the supervised hours while continuing loader shifts. In 2032, after thinking AI arrives, I'd check whether the mine is actually reducing driver hours and send applications to those shops if it is. By 2034 I'd be looking for paid repair work before robots take the driving shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel wary rather than trapped; five years gives me room to try. The hard part is keeping the mortgage paid while I'm still a beginner at something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make one repair place worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written wage, a trainer who actually has time, and shifts that let one of us collect the children. A course certificate without paid hours wouldn't get the mortgage paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound hopeful and doubtful at once. Which wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chance to train wins if the numbers work. I have used new tools before, but I don't confuse being quick with an app and knowing how to rebuild a hydraulic line.

say: I would say **five years** permits questions, while desk tasks change in 2031 and mining robots follow around 2034.
I would demand a **real job plan** from the mine.
think: I could learn repair, but my **junior grade** offers no guarantee of work through 2034.
At 48, the **mortgage** will still need wages, not a certificate alone.
do: Compare **paid trainee places** at the mine and ring road shops this winter.
Enrol if wages and supervised hours work while **continuing loader shifts**.
Check driver hours in 2032 and send **repair applications** if they fall.
feel: **Wary**, with enough time to try a paid route into repair.
S3.quote: A course certificate without paid hours wouldn't get the mortgage paid.
fieldNote: Her adaptability is practical: she wants **supervised wages** rather than a certificate with no route to income.
The children become teenagers by 2034; Elena still counts **collection shifts** in any job move.

steps.text: Compare paid repair trainee places at the mine and ring road shops
Continue loader shifts while taking supervised repair hours if paid
Send repair shop applications in 2032 if driver hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives ordinary workers time to plan if the mine shows us the plan early. Thinking AI could run paperwork in 2036, and robots able to drive loaders arrive around 2039; those are two different dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036 and 56 in 2039, I can't say I'll simply retire when robots take the driving. The children should be grown by then, so school costs should be behind us, but the mortgage balance and our health are unknown. I could build a second skill while the mine still pays me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the mine's repair training schedule at my next review and put a fixed amount from each normal wage into the mortgage reserve. Each year I'd check whether the training led to paid work, not just a badge. In 2037, the first year after thinking AI, I'd keep driving while asking for repair shifts; before 2039 I'd apply to shops if those hours don't materialise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more measured with ten years, though I don't feel safe for life. A date on a card can't promise my health or Marco's work will cooperate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you set aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd begin with what remains after the mortgage and the children's regular costs, perhaps the price of one takeaway meal each week. I would increase it only after seeing three months of actual wages and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want the children to follow you into mining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to see the work honestly before choosing any trade. I like the job, but I wouldn't tell them the loader seat will be waiting forever.

say: I would say **2036 and 2039** mean different changes for office tasks and loader work.
I would ask for the mine’s **training plan** early.
think: At 56 in 2039, I cannot assume **retirement** will replace my wages.
Grown children may cost less, but the **mortgage balance** remains uncertain.
do: Request the **repair schedule** at my next mine review.
Put a small fixed sum from normal wages into the **mortgage reserve**.
Keep driving in 2037 and seek **repair shifts** before robots reach the pit.
feel: **Measured** with more time, without expecting lifelong safety.
S4.quote: I like the job, but I wouldn't tell them the loader seat will be waiting forever.
fieldNote: A longer runway lets Elena build a **repair skill** while her present loader wages continue.
She does not turn grown children into current school costs or assume **retirement income** at 56.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because there is barely time to earn a second skill before robots reach the pit in 2031. A paid repair place with supervised hours and a clear wage would help more than another poster. I need to know whether I can carry the mortgage through training.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who covers school pickup when a training shift runs late. Marco and I can rearrange some days, but the family has to count that time. Any plan that treats family time as free has missed half the cost.

headlineQuote: Any plan that treats family time as free has missed half the cost.
portrait: Elena is a **43-year-old junior miner** who drives a loader and still checks uncertain calls with senior operators.
Her **mortgage and children** make paid training essential even though she learns tools quickly.
She treats the **three-year robot lag** as time to build repair skills, not as permanent protection.
A decade permits a **small reserve**, but she never assumes retirement wages at 56.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** because capable mining robots arrive around 2031 before she can reliably retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid repair apprenticeship** with supervised hours and a stated wage would let her keep paying the mortgage.
